ta-l1d29q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 29. Having treated innascibility, a property of a person but not personal, Lombard treats common spiration, which is neither a property of one person, since it belongs to two, nor personal, since it constitutes no person, designated when Father and Son are called principle of the Holy Spirit. He shows how 'principle' is said of God, and then, since it is said both temporally and eternally, how things are said of God from time (Dist. 30). He shows how many ways God is called principle: of creatures, from time and common to the whole Trinity by an operation in the creature; and of divine persons, the Father of the Son, and Father and Son of the Spirit, eternally and notionally, not essentially. He identifies the notion by which the Father is principle of the Son and that by which both are one principle of the Spirit, for which 'we have no name'. Four articles are announced: whether one person is principle of another; whether 'principle' is univocal of God with respect to persons and creatures; whether Father and Son are principle of the Spirit by the same notion; and whether they can be called one principle of him.
claims: Common spiration is neither a property of one person nor personal.
God is principle of creatures temporally and commonly, and of persons eternally and notionally.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e128.summary: First argument that one person is not principle of another. 'Principium' is imposed from priority, as the name sounds, and there is no prior and posterior among the divine persons (Dist. 9).
claims: Principle implies priority.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e131.summary: Second argument. A principle seems to be a cause, since 'cause' and 'principle' are said in as many ways (Metaphysics 5), and nothing is caused in the divine persons.
claims: Principle is cause.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e134.summary: Third argument. One person is principle of another only by giving being, and such a principle is operative or effective, but no person is called maker or worker of another.
claims: Giving being is efficient causality.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e138.summary: Sed contra. The text says the Father is principle of the whole deity.
claims: The Father is principle of the whole deity.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e141.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever something originates from is its principle, and one person originates from another.
claims: Origin implies principle.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e144.summary: Thomas's determination. To signify the origin of the divine persons we must use names fitting its mode, since speech should be subject to the thing (Hilary). In this origin the whole essence of one is received in another, so the three have numerically one essence and one being. So 'cause' does not fit, for two reasons: every cause is either outside the thing's essence (efficient, final) or part of it (matter, form); and every cause has the order of principle to the being of its effect, constituted by it, but the Father has no such order to the Son's being, any more than to his own, since they have one being. So the Father is not cause of the Son but principle, since 'principle' says an order of origin absolutely, determining no mode foreign to the origin of the persons. Some principles are not outside the essence of what they originate, like the point from which a line flows, and some have no influence on its being, like the starting point of a motion or morning as principle of the day. 'Author' adds to principle not being from another, so only the Father is called author, though the Son is also called principle notionally.
claims: The Father is principle, not cause, of the Son, since they share one essence and being.
'Principle' says order of origin absolutely; 'author' adds not being from another.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e147.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Principle' was imposed as found in creatures, where a principle is in some way prior to what it originates, so it is imposed from priority, but it was imposed to signify that from which something is. So though its mode of signifying does not fit God, as with other names we imposed, the thing signified fits most properly.
claims: 'Principle' signifies that from which something is; priority belongs only to its mode of signifying.
concepts: id a quo vs. id ad quod nomen imponitur

ta-l1d29q1-d1e150.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although the Father is called principle of the Son, he should not be called cause except improperly, as Chrysostom uses it, since principle is wider than cause and cause wider than element (the Commentator), so every cause is a principle but not conversely.
claims: Every cause is a principle, not conversely; the Father is cause of the Son only improperly.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e153.summary: Reply to the third argument. Making and operating always terminate in the thing's being, so the Son cannot be called made or worked by the Father, with whom he has one being, but only begotten, by origin of person.
claims: The Son is begotten, not made, since he shares the Father's being.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e170.summary: First argument that 'principle' is univocal for God as principle of a divine person and of creatures. Basil says receiving from the Father the Son has in common with every creature, but having by nature is proper to the Son, and the character of principle is founded on origin.
claims: Receiving from the Father is common to Son and creatures.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e173.summary: Second argument. Lombard divides principle into principle not from a principle, principle from a principle, and principle from both, which must include principle relative to creatures and to persons, and would be unscientific if 'principle' were equivocal.
claims: Lombard's division requires a univocal 'principle'.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e176.summary: Sed contra. Nothing is univocal of eternal and temporal, and principle of creatures is temporal while principle of a person is eternal.
claims: Eternal and temporal share nothing univocally.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e179.summary: Second sed contra. The Father is principle of the Son by generation, of the Spirit by spiration, and of creatures by creation, which are different characters of origin.
claims: Different modes of origin make 'principle' equivocal.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e188.summary: A further question: in which sense is 'principle' said primarily? It seems with respect to creatures, since the essential is conceptually prior to the notional and the common to the proper, and being principle of creatures is essential and common to the Trinity.
claims: The essential is prior to the notional.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e191.summary: Sed contra. The eternal is prior to the temporal, and principle of a person is eternal, of creatures temporal.
claims: Eternal is prior to temporal.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e200.summary: Thomas's determination on univocity. The same judgement holds of principle and of the origin it is founded on. Origin can be considered by its common character, something being from something, and so one character is common to the origin of persons and of creatures, by analogy, not univocity, and likewise 'principle'. Or it can be considered by its determinate mode, and then there are different special characters of origin and principle, but this does not make equivocation, since, as the Philosopher says, the concept of animal in each species is different.
claims: 'Principle' is common to persons and creatures by analogy.
Special modes of origin differ without making the term equivocal.
concepts: common vs. special characters of origin

ta-l1d29q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the first argument. Principle is common by analogy, not univocity.
claims: Principle is analogical.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the second argument. Lombard's division takes principle by its common character, which is one, not by the special ones, which differ.
claims: The division uses the common analogical character.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the third argument. Although nothing is univocal of eternal and temporal, something is common by analogy.
claims: Eternal and temporal share by analogy.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e213.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The argument concerns the special characters of origin, which do not make equivocation.
claims: Special modes do not create equivocation.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e223.summary: Thomas's determination on priority. The procession of creatures is modelled on that of the divine persons, so absolutely 'principle' is said first with respect to a person. But in principle as said of creatures one can consider the temporal relation itself and what it is founded on, divine power and operation, which have the character of principle only habitually. Considered the second way, principle of creatures is prior to principle of a divine person, which is founded on a property, in the way the essential is conceptually prior to the notional, but only in some respect.
claims: Absolutely, 'principle' is said first of the persons, whose procession exemplifies creation.
In some respect, as founded on divine power, principle of creatures is prior.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e239.summary: First argument that Father and Son do not have one property by which they are principle of the Spirit. Properties take unity and multitude from their supposits, and Father and Son are not one supposit.
claims: Properties are multiplied by supposits.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e242.summary: Second argument. Nothing is both uniting and distinguishing, and the notions distinguish, so no notion unites Father and Son.
claims: Notions distinguish.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e245.summary: Third argument. Things united in nature and property are more one than those united in nature only, and Father and Son are not more one than Father and Spirit, who share only nature.
claims: Shared notion would make Father and Son more one.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e249.summary: Fourth argument. What a property is in is closer to it than what it is toward, and properties in one person are several by being toward different terms (generation to the Son, spiration to the Spirit), so much more would they be two by being in two persons.
claims: Subject is closer to a property than term.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e252.summary: Sed contra from Anselm: Father and Son are one in everything where opposition of relation does not distinguish them, and in common spiration they are not opposed, so it is numerically one in both.
claims: Unopposed features are one in Father and Son.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e255.summary: Thomas's determination. Father and Son have numerically one notion as principle of the Spirit, as the text says. Distinction of things by form occurs only two ways: a common character distinguished by several special characters, as a genus into species; or a specific nature distinguished numerically into many. The second cannot be in God, for two reasons: numerical multiplication within a species comes not from something formal but from divided matter, since the lowest species is constituted by the last constitutive form, and there is no matter in God; and a specific nature is multiplied only by the being it has in different things, since the whole quiddity is complete in the species, and in God there is only one being. So nothing said by a special character can be numerically multiplied in God. Whatever is in God either remains undistinguished and numerically one, like the nature common to the three, or has a common character distinguishable by special characters, as relation is common to the three yet not numerically one relation, being different by special character. Since common spiration names a special character of principle by a special mode of origin, it must be numerically one in Father and Son.
claims: Common spiration is numerically one notion in Father and Son.
Nothing of a special character is numerically multiplied in God, for lack of matter and of plural being.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e258.summary: Reply to the first argument. In creatures supposits are distinct by being, so their properties are distinct by being too. In the divine supposits there is one being, so a property cannot be multiplied by being but only by its special character.
claims: In God properties are not multiplied by being.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e261.summary: Reply to the second argument. Something cannot be uniting and distinguishing in the same respect and toward the same, so common spiration distinguishes the Father from the Spirit but unites him with the Son.
claims: Common spiration unites Father and Son and distinguishes them from the Spirit.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e264.summary: Reply to the third argument. According to Augustine, equality and inequality are not found by relations of origin, so the Father's sharing a notion with the Son does not make him more one with the Son than with the Spirit, only one in more things.
claims: Shared notions do not make greater unity, only unity in more.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e268.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A relative property, by its being, is closer to its supposit than to its term, so if there were variation by being it would come from the supposits. But by the concept of relation it is toward another, and so the special character of relation is distinguished as it refers to different terms.
claims: Relations are distinguished by their terms, not by being.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e281.summary: First argument that Father and Son are not one principle of the Spirit. Either they are one that is the Father, so the Son is the Father, or one that is not the Father, so the Father is not the Father.
claims: A dilemma against one principle.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e284.summary: Second argument. Because the three are one principle of creatures we say they are one Creator, but we do not say Father and Son are one Spirator.
claims: They are not 'one spirator'.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e287.summary: Third argument. Unity causes identity, and Father and Son are not called the same principle of the Spirit.
claims: Not 'the same principle'.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e291.summary: Sed contra. Father and Son are one in all things where opposition of relation does not distinguish and where 'this from that' is said, and the Son is principle from principle, so they are one principle.
claims: Principle from principle implies one principle.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e294.summary: Second sed contra. One thing has one principle, and the Spirit is one.
claims: One effect, one principle.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e297.summary: Thomas's determination. All who confess the Spirit proceeds from both say Father and Son are one principle of him, but they explain it differently. Some say 'one' designates only unity of proportion, since Father and Son relate alike to the Spirit as spirating; this is insufficient, since they also agree by proportion in being supposits, yet are not one supposit. Others say it designates unity of nature, relying on Anselm, who says they spirate the Spirit as each is God; but unless more is said, the Spirit would not be excluded from the unity of notional principle, since he is not excluded from unity of nature. Others say it designates unity of notion, which seems fitting, since in substantive names unity and plurality follow the form signified (one God by unity of divine nature), and the form 'principle' signifies, taken personally, is the notion or property itself, as 'Father' signifies paternity, so unity of principle follows unity of notion. To save Anselm, one can also say it signifies unity in spirative power, which is the divine nature under the character of such a property, the principle of personal operation (Dist. 11).
claims: Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by unity of notion.
Alternatively, by unity of spirative power, the nature under the notion.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e300.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Either one that is the Father or one that is not the Father' is not a division by contradictories, so both are false. What is true is that they are not one that is only the Father, but one that is Father and Son, as they are one God who is Father and Son.
claims: The dilemma is not exhaustive; they are one principle who is Father and Son.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e303.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though they are called one principle, they are not called one spirating or one spirator, since such names are imposed from acts, which always signify adjectivally, and in pluralizing them the plurality of supposits counts, not of the form signified (Dist. 16). Creation differs from spiration: spiration presupposes distinction of supposits and is in some way from several supposits as distinct, being a personal operation, while creation is the work of the divine essence and so of an undistinguished supposit, as the essence is signified as 'what is' by 'God'. So as Father and Son are one, one God, they are one Creator, but not one creating, since the participle is adjectival.
claims: Names from acts pluralize by supposits; 'one spirator' is not said, but 'one Creator' is, since creation is the essence's work.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e306.summary: Reply to the third argument. It is not commonly granted that they are the same principle, since by the force of the article unity of supposit is included, as Lombard says God did not beget himself as God nor another God. Some say Father and Son are the same God and the same principle, since 'same' is an adjective that posits not absolute identity but identity relative to the term it modifies, and in that sense it can be granted.
claims: 'The same principle' is usually avoided as implying one supposit, though it can be granted with 'same' taken adjectivally.

ta-l1d29q1-d1e315.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'The Father is principle of the whole deity' seems false, whether 'deity' means essence (the Father is not principle of the essence, and wholeness needs distinct parts) or persons (he is not principle of himself). It can be taken either way: as essence, 'whole' means perfection of nature, not integrity of parts, and he is principle of deity not by begetting or spirating it but by communicating it, so that deity is had; in that sense the Son could also be principle of the whole divinity, since perfect divinity is in the Spirit from him, except that not by every mode of communication and not by generation. As the persons, it is plainer: he is quasi-principle from whom the others flow, as a point is principle of the whole line though not of itself. (2) Lombard's 'or better, of divinity' is better because 'deity' comes from 'God', signifying per se and essentially the one having divinity, while 'divinity' comes from 'divine', a denominative that can signify participation, as the Philosopher calls the perpetuity of species divine, so 'divinity' better designates singular excellence. (3) 'All natures' means all substances, and 'what are naturally' properties and natural operations. (4) 'He confesses the Son's origin from a beginning' means from the Father, and lest 'beginning' be taken for a beginning of duration he adds 'not from a beginning' of duration 'but from the unbegun', the initiating principle, the Father; the Son is not 'through himself' in the sense of 'from himself'.
claims: The Father is principle of the whole deity by communicating it, and of the persons as the one from whom they flow.
The Son's origin is from a principle, not from a beginning of duration.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e165.summary: The first quaestiuncula of Article 2 gives arguments that 'principle' is univocal for persons and creatures, from Basil and from Lombard's division, and contrary arguments from the eternal–temporal gap and the diversity of origins.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e183.summary: The second quaestiuncula of Article 2 asks whether 'principle' is said first of creatures, since the essential precedes the notional, or of persons, since the eternal precedes the temporal.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e195.summary: Thomas's solution to the first quaestiuncula holds that 'principle', like origin, is common to persons and creatures by analogy, not univocity, while the special modes of origin differ without making it equivocal.
claims: 'Principle' is analogical.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e218.summary: Thomas's solution to the second quaestiuncula holds that 'principle' is said first of the persons absolutely, since their procession exemplifies creation, though in some respect, as founded on divine power, principle of creatures is prior.
claims: Principle of persons is prior absolutely.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 29 introduces Lombard's treatment of common spiration, neither a property of one person nor personal, and of the senses of 'principle', of creatures temporally and of persons eternally. It announces four articles: whether one person is principle of another, whether 'principle' is univocal for persons and creatures, whether Father and Son spirate by one notion, and whether they are one principle.
claims: Common spiration is neither proper nor personal.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e120.summary: Article 1 holds that one divine person is principle of another, but not cause, since the persons share one essence and being and every cause is outside or part of the essence and orders to its effect's being. 'Principle' says order of origin absolutely; 'author' adds not being from another and fits only the Father. Priority belongs only to the mode of signifying of 'principle', every cause is a principle but not conversely, and the Son is begotten, not made.
claims: The Father is principle, not cause, of the Son.
Only the Father is author.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e157.summary: Article 2, in two quaestiunculae, holds that 'principle' is common to persons and creatures by analogy, not univocity, with special modes of origin not causing equivocation. Absolutely it is said first of the persons, whose procession exemplifies that of creatures, though principle of creatures is prior in some respect, as founded on essential power.
claims: 'Principle' is analogical and said first of the persons.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e231.summary: Article 3 holds that common spiration is numerically one notion in Father and Son. Nothing with a special character can be numerically multiplied in God, since there is no matter and only one being. So whatever is in God is either numerically one or a common character distinguished by special ones. Common spiration unites Father and Son while distinguishing them from the Spirit, without making them more one, and relations are distinguished by their terms, not by being.
claims: Common spiration is one in number in Father and Son.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e273.summary: Article 4 holds that Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by unity of notion, or by unity of spirative power, rejecting the views from unity of proportion or of nature alone. They are not one only-Father but one Father-and-Son. They are not 'one spirator', since names from personal acts pluralize by supposits, though they are 'one Creator', since creation is the essence's work. 'The same principle' is usually avoided.
claims: Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by one notion.
They are one Creator but not one spirator.

ta-l1d29q1-Dd1e310.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 29 explains how the Father is principle of the whole deity, by communicating the essence and as source of the persons. It prefers 'divinity' to 'deity' for singular excellence and reads the Son's origin as from the unbegun principle, not from a beginning of duration.
claims: The Father is principle of the whole deity by communicating it.

ta-l1d29q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 29 treats 'principle' in God. Article 1 holds that one person is principle of another but not cause, since they share one essence and being, and that only the Father is author. Article 2 holds that 'principle' is analogical between persons and creatures and is said first of the persons absolutely. Article 3 holds that common spiration is numerically one notion in Father and Son, since nothing of a special character is numerically multiplied in God. Article 4 holds that Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by unity of notion, and one Creator but not one spirator.
claims: The Father is principle, not cause, of the Son.
'Principle' is analogical, said first of the persons.
Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by one notion of common spiration.
